rows.text: People can talk to their neighbours and join activities. They can also respect other religions. Singapore has many races living in the same estates.

One way is to take part in each other's festivals. For example, a family can accept a neighbour's invitation to a Hari Raya open house. They eat together and can ask about the fast and the customs. This replaces guesses about the other group with what they have seen for themselves, so there is more understanding. Another way is to respect other religions.

One way is to take part in each other's festivals. For example, a family can accept a neighbour's invitation to a Hari Raya open house. They eat together and can ask about the fast and the customs. This replaces guesses about the other group with what they have seen for themselves, so there is more understanding. A second way is to speak up against stereotypes. For example, when a classmate jokes that one race is lazy, a student can say that it is not true and not funny. This stops a false idea from spreading in the group, so others learn to judge people by what they do and not by their race.
I agree because shared experiences are important and people should mix around. Policies are also important in Singapore.

Shared experiences build harmony. For example, in a school CCA, students of different races train together for months and depend on each other to win. They come to trust each other as teammates, so race matters less to them and friendships form across groups.

Shared experiences build harmony. For example, in a school CCA, students of different races train together for months and depend on each other to win. They come to trust each other as teammates, so race matters less to them and friendships form across groups. Government policies also build harmony. For example, the Ethnic Integration Policy sets a limit for each race in every HDB block. This prevents one-race estates, so people meet neighbours of other races every day in the lifts and corridors and cannot live apart.

Shared experiences build harmony. For example, in a school CCA, students of different races train together for months and depend on each other to win. They come to trust each other as teammates, so race matters less to them and friendships form across groups. Government policies also build harmony. For example, the Ethnic Integration Policy sets a limit for each race in every HDB block. This prevents one-race estates, so people meet neighbours of other races every day and cannot live apart. Policies do more, because shared experiences depend on them. Students of different races are in the same CCA, and neighbours meet at the same lift, only because policies put them in the same schools and blocks first. Without the policy, most people would stay with their own group and the shared experiences would not happen. So I disagree: experiences build the friendships, but policy is what makes them possible.
Citizens can help directly and give feedback so that policies fit people's needs. They can volunteer and donate.

One way is to volunteer with a group that serves people in need. For example, volunteers at a food charity pack and deliver rations to elderly people living alone every week. The government gives financial help but cannot visit every home, so the volunteers meet a need that would be missed. Citizens can also give feedback.

One way is to volunteer with a group that serves people in need. For example, volunteers at a food charity pack and deliver rations to elderly people living alone every week. The government gives financial help but cannot visit every home, so the volunteers meet a need that would be missed. A second way is to give feedback on policies. For example, citizens can give their views in a public consultation, such as those run by REACH, before a policy is changed. The government learns how the policy affects ordinary people, so it can adjust the policy to fit their needs better.
I disagree. Organised groups are bigger than individuals so they are better. Individuals can also help.

Individuals meet needs quickly. For example, a resident who notices that an elderly neighbour has not been seen for days can knock on the door and call for help. No form or approval is needed, so the need is met at once, before any organisation knows about it.

Individuals meet needs quickly. For example, a resident who notices that an elderly neighbour has not been seen for days can knock on the door and call for help. No form or approval is needed, so the need is met at once, before any organisation knows about it. Organised groups also meet needs. For example, a family service centre has trained social workers and funding. It can take on a long case, such as a family in debt, and follow it for months, so needs that take skill and time are met properly.

Individuals meet needs quickly. For example, a resident who notices that an elderly neighbour has not been seen for days can knock on the door and call for help. No form or approval is needed, so the need is met at once, before any organisation knows about it. Organised groups also meet needs. For example, a family service centre has trained social workers and funding. It can take on a long case, such as a family in debt, and follow it for months, so needs that take skill and time are met properly. Organised groups do more, judged by how many people they reach and for how long. An individual helps the few people he happens to know, and the help stops when he is busy. A group can serve thousands and carries on when one volunteer leaves. So I disagree: individuals are faster, but organised groups meet more needs and keep meeting them.
Globalisation links countries through trade, travel and technology. Workers are affected because goods and people move faster. Some gain and some lose.

One way is that workers may lose their jobs. For example, a company can move its factory to a country where wages are lower. The workers in the first country are no longer needed and are retrenched, so they lose their income. Another way is more opportunities.

One way is that workers may lose their jobs. For example, a company can move its factory to a country where wages are lower. The workers in the first country are no longer needed and are retrenched, so they lose their income. A second way is that workers get more job opportunities. For example, when foreign technology firms set up regional offices in Singapore, they hire local staff. Workers have more employers to choose from, so those with the right skills can earn higher pay.
I agree because money is important to a country. Culture is also changing because of globalisation, like food and music.

The economic effects matter. For example, Singapore has few natural resources and earns its living by trading with the world, and foreign companies invest here. This creates jobs and income for its people, so the country can pay for schools and hospitals.

This creates jobs and income for its people, so the country can pay for schools and hospitals. The cultural effects matter too. For example, young people watch foreign shows and follow global brands, and fewer speak dialects or keep traditional customs. Local culture weakens, so people may feel less attached to their own country and its past.

Local culture weakens, so people may feel less attached to their own country and its past. The economic effects matter more, because a country's survival rests on them. If trade and investment stop, people lose their jobs at once. Cultural change is slower, and a country can respond to it, for example by teaching heritage in schools. A country with a strong economy also has the money to protect its culture. So I agree: both matter, but the economic effects decide whether the country can do anything else.
